items.readable_text:
Content:
The roots of a function are the values of the input [MATH: x] for which the function equals zero. For this reason, roots are sometimes also called zeros.

Content:
Algebraically, the roots of a function are the solutions for [MATH: x] in the following equation:

Content:
[MATH: f(x)=0]

Content:
For example, if [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}x+1,] then we can find the roots by solving the equation [MATH: f(x) = 0,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: f(x)|= 0; (1)/(2)x + 1|= 0; (1)/(2)x|= − 1; x|= − 2]

Content:
So, this function has a single root: [MATH: x=-2.]

Content:
Graphically, the roots of a function are the [MATH: x]-intercepts. For example, for the graph of [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{2}x+1] shown below, we can see that the function intercepts the [MATH: x]-axis at [MATH: x=-2.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3f5b6d9c387df61cdd1eddff293dae51]

Content:
When shown on a graph, the roots of a function are also called the [MATH: \boldsymbol x]-intercepts.
